ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *wekʷ-der. Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs Proto-Italic *wōks Latin vōx Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Latin vōcālisbor. Middle English vocal English vocal Late Middle English vocal, borrowed from Latin vōcālis (“uttering a voice, sounding, speaking”), from vōx (“a voice, sound, tone”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of vowel and vocalis. Compare Old French vocal.

senses.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the human voice or speech.
Used in the production of speech sounds.
Relating to, composed or arranged for, or sung by the human voice.

Consisting of, or characterized by, voice, or tone produced in the larynx, which may be modified, either by resonance, as in the case of the vowels, or by obstructive action, as in certain consonants, such as v, l, etc., or by both, as in the nasals m, n, ng.
Synonym of vocalic.
Uttered or modulated by the voice; expressed in words.
ex: vocal melody, vocal prayer, vocal worship

senses.d: Expressing opinions or feelings freely, loudly, or insistently.
ex: The protesters were very vocal in their message to the mayor.

senses.d: Having or exercising the power of producing voice, speech, or sound.
ex:
To hill or valley, fountain, or fresh shade,
Made vocal by my song.

The tide flows down, the wave again
⁠Is vocal in its wooded walls:
⁠My deeper anguish also falls,
And I can speak a little then.

senses.d: Synonym of expressive.
Full of voices.
A vocal sound; specifically, a purely vocal element of speech, unmodified except by resonance; a vowel or a diphthong; a tonic element; a tonic.
A part of a piece of music that is sung.
ex: Best cuts: "The Evil Dude," "Kung Fu, Too!" "Mama Love," "New Orleans" (with a punchy vocal by Teresa Brewer).

senses.d: A musical performance involving singing.
A man in the Roman Catholic Church who has a right to vote in certain elections.

grp.label: of or pertaining to the voice or speech
characterized by voice or tone produced in the larynx
uttered or modulated by the voice

ety.text: Inherited from Old French vocal, borrowed from Latin vōcālis. Doublet of voyelle.
Learned borrowing from Latin vōcālis (“speaking, sounding”). By surface analysis, voc(e) (“voice”) + -ale (“-al”, adjective-forming derivational suffix).

senses.d: A usually alphabetized and explained collection of words e.g. of a particular field, or prepared for a specific purpose, often for learning.
The collection of words a person knows and uses.
ex: My Russian vocabulary is very limited.

senses.d: The stock of words used in a particular field.
ex: The vocabulary of social sciences is often incomprehensible to ordinary people.

senses.d: The words of a language collectively; lexis.
ex: The vocabulary of any language is influenced by contacts with other cultures.

senses.d: A range of artistic or stylistic forms or techniques.
